descriptions: Before creation the Goddess alone existed; she produced the cosmic egg and the gods (Bahvṛca Upaniṣad; Devī Gītā 7.32).
She is eternal and the world is her form; yet for the gods' sake she is born again and again (Devī Māhātmya 1).
She abides in all beings as consciousness, intelligence, sleep, hunger, power, faith, peace, compassion and mother (Devī Māhātmya 5).
She is Mahāmāyā, who drags even the minds of the wise into delusion, and when pleased grants liberation (Devī Māhātmya 1).
She declares herself Brahman, of the nature of consciousness (Devī Upaniṣad).
negations: nirguṇā, niṣkalā, nirākārā — without qualities, parts or form (Lalitā Sahasranāma 43-45)
beyond the three gods' consorts, 'a certain fourth', hard to reach, of boundless greatness (Saundaryalaharī 98)
relation_to_self: She is the inner self of all; 'she is the self' (Bahvṛca); she abides in beings as consciousness.
relation_to_world: The world is her manifestation and her body; she creates, sustains and withdraws it and deludes and liberates through her power of māyā.
caveat: Śāktas name the ultimate as the feminine Śakti, the Mother, and many resist readings that make her a mere attribute of a male god or that make the world she manifests unreal; but Śākta texts themselves identify her with the Brahman of the Upaniṣads and declare all goddesses her forms, which fits the one-truth reading.

descriptions: Tripurā is the supreme, whose nature is the fusion (sāmarasya) of light (prakāśa) and self-awareness (vimarśa) (Amṛtānanda on Yoginīhṛdaya 1.6).

Maheśa, whose body is pure light, holds self-awareness within; the primal Śakti is the stainless mirror in which Śiva knows himself; their union is the great point (mahābindu) and the 'I' (Kāmakalāvilāsa 1-5).
She is consciousness-power (citśakti) and also the power of the insentient (Lalitā Sahasranāma 90).
She is 'the form of the oneness of Śiva and Śakti' and dwells in the king of cakras (Lalitā Sahasranāma 182-183).
When the supreme Śakti, by her own will, beholds her own vibrancy, the cakra (the universe) arises (Yoginīhṛdaya 1.9-10).
negations: nirguṇā, niṣkalā, nirupādhi — beyond qualities, parts and limiting adjuncts (Lalitā Sahasranāma 43-45)
beyond the reach of mind and speech (manovācām agocarā, Lalitā Sahasranāma 89)
relation_to_self: The Goddess is one's own self: the jīva is Śiva clothed in coverings, Paraśiva is the uncovered (PKS 1.5); worship is the contemplation of the non-difference of knower, knowing and known (Bhāvanā Upaniṣad).
relation_to_world: The universe of thirty-six principles is the Śrīcakra, her self-expansion; she herself becomes mind, space, air, fire, water and earth, and nothing lies beyond her (Saundaryalaharī 35).
caveat: Śrīvidyā holds that the Goddess in union with Śiva is the one ultimate, and treats the one-truth principle as its own (she is worshipped by all the gods). It would reject a reading that makes Lalitā one symbol among equals or that denies the reality of her power. Within the tradition the Samaya school insists on the strict equality of Śiva and Śakti, while uttara-Kaula readings hold Śakti alone; Bhāskararāya's gloss 'substratum of the false world' (name 735) leans to Advaita, while the Kāmakalāvilāsa speaks of real manifestation — these differences are recorded, not erased.

descriptions: Śiva and Śakti are equal in primacy, sharing a fivefold equality of seat, state, action, form and name (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 41).
The Goddess worshipped in the thousand-petalled lotus, where the Śrīcakra is the moon-disc (Lakṣmīdhara on SL 10).
relation_to_self: The Goddess is realized within, in the space of the heart and the crown; the Samayin identifies the cakra with his own inner space.
relation_to_world: The world is produced by the Śiva-Śakti pair acting together as father and mother (SL 41).
caveat: The Samaya school rejects the uttara-Kaula view that only the Śakti principle exists and the pūrva-Kaula view that makes Śiva her body alone; any reconciliation with Kaula views must record this objection.

descriptions: Tripurā is the fusion of prakāśa and vimarśa (Dīpikā on YH 1.6).
The kāmakalā — two bindus, white and red, and their union — is the Goddess's own form; knowing it one becomes Mahātripurasundarī (Kāmakalāvilāsa 6-8).
relation_to_self: Knowledge of the cakra-saṅketa makes one liberated while living, abiding in the I-sense of Śiva (YH 1.86 with the Dīpikā).
relation_to_world: The cakra of thirty-six principles unfolds when Śakti beholds her own vibrancy (YH 1.9-10).
caveat: This line holds the Goddess is both Kaula and Samaya and that outer worship is part of the path even for the knower; it would not accept a Samaya reconciliation that declares Kaula worship outside the Veda.
